title: Wild rice vs. brown rice: nutrition comparison

seo.title: Wild rice vs. brown rice: nutrition comparison
seo.meta_description: Compare cooked wild rice and brown rice per 100 g for calories, protein, carbs, fat and fiber, plus botanical and culinary differences.
seo.search_intent: Compare wild rice and brown rice nutrition

excerpt: Wild rice is Zizania, not a variety of brown rice. Per 100 g cooked it provides more protein in USDA reference data, while the fiber difference is small.
content_html:
Wild rice and brown rice often occupy the same part of the plate, but they are not two versions of the same grain. Brown rice is Oryza sativa with the bran and germ retained. Wild rice comes from Zizania species, aquatic grasses native to North America whose seeds are cooked and used much like rice.

There are nutritional differences, but the comparison only makes sense on the same cooked-weight basis. Comparing dry grain with a cooked cup mostly measures water absorption.

Nutrition per 100 g cooked

Using USDA reference data for cooked wild rice without added fat and cooked long-grain brown rice:

Per 100 g cookedWild riceBrown rice
Calories~100 kcal123 kcal
Protein~4.0 g2.7 g
Carbohydrate~21.2 g25.6 g
Fat~0.3 g1.0 g
Fiber~1.8 g1.6 g

Protein is the clearest difference: about 4.0 g versus 2.7 g per 100 g, roughly 45% more protein in the wild rice reference. That does not turn wild rice into a high-protein food—a 150 g portion would contain about 6 g—but it is a meaningful relative difference.

Wild rice also comes in lower in calories and carbohydrate per 100 g cooked in these records. Some of that reflects how much water the cooked grains hold, which is why these numbers are best read as “what is in 100 g on the plate,” not as a universal dry-grain ranking.

Does wild rice have much more fiber?

Not in this comparison. The values are about 1.8 g versus 1.6 g per 100 g. At a 150 g cooked serving, that works out to roughly 2.7 g versus 2.4 g. Wild rice is slightly higher, but the gap is only about 0.3 g per 150 g serving.

Texture may matter more than small nutrient gaps

Brown rice is relatively tender and neutral, with a mild nutty character. Wild rice is firmer, darker, and more assertive. It works especially well in salads, stuffing, soups, and grain blends.

One shopping detail matters: many packages called “wild rice blend” contain white rice, brown rice, and only a fraction of actual wild rice. The table above is for wild rice itself. A blend will reflect whatever proportions are in the bag.

Which one should you choose?

Wild rice is a good pick if you want a chewier grain and a little more protein per cooked weight. Brown rice is an easy, versatile whole grain and is usually simpler to find and less expensive. The fiber difference is too small here to make that the deciding factor.

For a complete meal, what you pair with the grain—beans, vegetables, fish, eggs, tofu, or another protein—usually changes the nutritional picture more than the small fiber difference between these two.

Bottom line

Wild rice is not simply darker brown rice; it is a different genus of grass. In USDA cooked-food reference data, it has more protein and somewhat less carbohydrate and energy per 100 g, while the fiber difference is modest. Compare equal cooked weights, then choose based on taste, texture, price, and the meal you are building.

faq.question: Is wild rice actually rice?
faq.answer: Not botanically. It comes from aquatic grasses in the genus Zizania, while cultivated rice is in the genus Oryza.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: In the USDA records compared here, cooked wild rice has about 4.0 g per 100 g versus 2.7 g in cooked brown rice—roughly 45% more.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: The difference is small in this comparison: about 1.8 g per 100 g for wild rice versus 1.6 g for brown rice.

faq.question: Is a wild-rice blend nutritionally the same?
faq.answer: No. Many blends contain white or brown rice plus a smaller amount of wild rice. Check the ingredient list and package nutrition facts.
